pos: v. (to run faster than; to outstrip in running)
etymology: A compound of out-, in the sense of surpassing, and run, Old English rinnan. The Greek protrecho means to run forward or ahead, from pro (before) and trecho (to run).
biblical_def: On the first day of the week two disciples run to the sepulchre and the Gospel records which arrived first: “So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre” (John 20:4). To outrun is to outstrip in running, and the detail is the kind of thing only an eyewitness notices and only a modest one records this way; John names himself as the other disciple throughout his Gospel and reports that he was the faster man without pressing any advantage from it. For he stooped down and looked in and waited, and Peter went in first; and then: “Then went in also that other disciple, which came first to the sepulchre, and he saw, and believed” (John 20:8). The running is not a race for honour but the natural haste of men who have heard that the body is gone. Paul uses the figure deliberately for the Christian life: “Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9:24). Speed to the empty tomb is a good instinct; it was the first morning of the resurrection.

webster_full: OUTRUN, v.t. To exceed in running; to run faster than another, and leave him behind.
To exceed; to go beyond; as, to let the tongue outrun the sense.

corruption_summary: Small eyewitness details in the resurrection accounts are treated as later embroidery, when their very smallness is what no inventor supplies.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments of the resurrection narratives explain details like this one as legendary accretion or as apologetic device, with the differences among the four accounts offered as evidence of invention. The dictionary holds the apostolic authorship of all four Gospels as traditionally ascribed, and holds the bodily resurrection on the third day as an event in history.

The detail itself argues against invention. A fabricator working for effect does not record that one disciple ran faster, then that he let the other go in first, then that the faster man believed on seeing the linen clothes. There is no doctrine riding on who won the footrace and no advantage claimed. It reads as it is: the memory of a man who was there, running in the half-light, breathing hard, who saw the grave clothes lying and believed before he had seen the Lord.

pos: v. (past tense of outgo; went faster than, arrived before)
etymology: Past tense of outgo, from out- (surpassing) and go. The Greek proerchomai means to go before or arrive ahead, from pro (before) and erchomai (to come).
biblical_def: When Christ withdrew with His disciples for rest, the crowd beat Him to the place: “And the people saw them departing, and many knew him, and ran afoot thither out of all cities, and outwent them, and came together unto him” (Mark 6:33). To outgo is to go faster and arrive first, and the picture is of thousands running the shoreline on foot while the boat crossed the water. The context makes the moment pointed. Christ had just said, “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat” (Mark 6:31). The rest He had planned for His disciples was taken from them by a crowd that would not be left behind. And His response is the thing the verse exists to show: “And Jesus, when he came out, saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd: and he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34). He did not resent the interruption. He saw shepherdless sheep, taught them, and then fed five thousand.

webster_full: OUTGO, v.t. To go beyond; to advance before in gait or pace.

corruption_summary: Christ's compassion in this scene is pressed into a doctrine of limitless availability that burns out His servants, or His withdrawal into a doctrine of self-care that never gets interrupted.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 6 is quoted on both sides of the modern argument about ministry and rest, and both sides take half. One half says Christ sought rest, therefore boundaries are holy and interruptions may be refused; the other says Christ taught the crowd anyway, therefore any limit is selfishness. The passage holds both without strain and subordinates both to something else.

Christ had deliberately planned rest for weary men who had no leisure to eat; the plan was good and He made it. The crowd overtook them, and He did not reclaim His plan but looked at the people and saw sheep without a shepherd. That order matters. Rest is a creature's due and a gift of the sabbath; compassion is the Shepherd's nature. A servant who never rests presumes; a servant who cannot be interrupted has not learned Mark 6:34.

etymology: A compound of over-, in the sense of beyond, and live. Overlive is the older form of outlive. The Hebrew phrase in Joshua 24:31 speaks of the elders who prolonged days after Joshua.
biblical_def: The book of Joshua closes with a measured statement about how long a generation's obedience lasted: “And Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that overlived Joshua, and which had known all the works of the LORD, that he had done for Israel” (Joshua 24:31). To overlive a man is to outlive him, and the verse names the exact limit of Israel's faithfulness: the lifetime of the men who had seen the works of God with their own eyes. Joshua himself had set the choice before them: “choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). The elders who overlived him held the line. And then the next book records the collapse in a single devastating sentence: “And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10). Firsthand memory is not transmissible. Only teaching is, and a generation that neglects to teach will be overlived by its own apostasy.

corruption_summary: Faith is assumed to pass down with the family or the institution, so that catechising is neglected and one generation's experience is expected to serve the next.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Joshua 24:31 and Judges 2:10 state together: obedience lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses, and the next generation knew not the LORD.

Churches and households repeat the failure in every era. A movement is born in genuine revival, the founders see God work, the institutions they build outlive them, and the grandchildren inherit the furniture without the faith. Scripture's remedy is relentless and unglamorous: teach these words diligently unto thy children, talk of them in the house and by the way, train them in the catechism and the confession, bring them under preaching. Experience cannot be bequeathed. Doctrine, taught and believed, can.

pos: v. (to drive too hard; to push beyond endurance)
etymology: A compound of over-, in the sense of excess, and drive, Old English drifan. The Hebrew daphaq means to beat or knock, hence to drive hard.
biblical_def: Jacob declines Esau's offer to travel together, and the reason he gives is pastoral: “And he said unto him, My lord knoweth that the children are tender, and the flocks and herds with young are with me: and if men should overdrive them one day, all the flock will die” (Genesis 33:13). To overdrive is to push a flock beyond what it can bear. Jacob names three vulnerable groups — tender children, nursing ewes, cattle with young — and states the consequence with no hedging: one hard day and the whole flock is lost. His alternative is the pace of the weakest: “I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure” (Genesis 33:14). Scripture makes this the pattern of God's own shepherding: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). The principle governs every pastor, father and employer. A flock is driven at the speed of the weakest member, or it is not driven at all but destroyed.

webster_full: OVERDRIVE, v.t. To drive too hard, or beyond strength.
DRIVE, v.t. To impel or urge forward by force; to force along.

corruption_summary: Zeal is measured by pace, so that pastors, parents and employers drive the strong and lose the weak, calling the casualties a lack of commitment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jacob's: the flock moves at the speed of the nursing ewe and the tender child, or it dies.

Ministries and households violate it constantly, usually in the name of vision. A programme is set at the pace of its most capable members; those who cannot keep up are quietly reclassified as uncommitted; and the attrition is read as refining rather than as loss. Jacob's arithmetic is blunter — one hard day and all the flock will die — and Isaiah tells us whose manner Jacob was imitating. The Shepherd of Israel carries lambs in His bosom and gently leads those that are with young. No under-shepherd has warrant to drive harder than that.

pos: n. pl. (covered couches carried by men or beasts; conveyances for the infirm or honoured)
etymology: From Old French litiere, from Latin lectus, a bed or couch. A litter is a portable bed, used for the sick, the aged and persons of rank. The Hebrew tsab denotes a covered conveyance.
biblical_def: The last chapter of Isaiah describes the gathering of the Gentiles and the carrying home of the dispersed: “And they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the LORD out of all nations upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, saith the LORD, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the LORD” (Isaiah 66:20). Litters are covered couches borne by beasts or men, the conveyance of those too weak to walk and of those too honoured to. The list is deliberately varied: horses for the strong, swift beasts for the fast, litters for the infirm. Nobody is left behind because of weakness. The verse before has described the sending: “I will send those that escape of them unto the nations... and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles” (Isaiah 66:19). Paul understood his own apostleship in exactly this language: “that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost” (Romans 15:16). The litter is the detail that makes the prophecy tender: the ingathering is paced for the weakest who are coming home.

corruption_summary: The ingathering of the nations is reassigned to a future Jewish political restoration with a rebuilt temple, or spiritualised until no actual peoples are gathered at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism reads Isaiah 66 as a programme for a restored national Israel with a functioning temple and sacrificial system in a millennial age. The dictionary rejects dispensationalism as a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, and rejects this reading because the New Testament has already told us how the chapter is being fulfilled: Paul takes the offering of the Gentiles as the description of his own missionary labour.

The opposite error empties the prophecy of flesh and blood. Isaiah names Tarshish, Lud, Tubal and Javan; real peoples, in real places, carried home on real animals and litters. The gathering is the great commission in prophetic dress: the nations brought in as an offering, acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Ghost, and the holy mountain is the church of the living God to which every believing Gentile has already come.

pos: n. pl. (inns, houses of public lodging; in the place-name The three taverns)
etymology: From Old French taverne, from Latin taberna, a hut, booth or shop. The Greek renders the Latin place-name Tres Tabernae, Three Taverns, a staging post on the Appian Way about thirty miles south of Rome.
biblical_def: Paul, a prisoner on the last stage of the road to Rome, is met by believers who had walked out to find him: “And from thence, when the brethren heard of us, they came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage” (Acts 28:15). The three taverns is a place-name, Tres Tabernae, a staging post on the Appian Way; a tavern in this sense is an inn or booth for travellers, not a drinking house in the modern sense. The verse is one of the most human in Acts. The apostle who had written the epistle to the Romans, survived a shipwreck and faced Caesar, is strengthened by the sight of a few brethren who had walked some thirty miles down a road to stand beside him. Luke records the two effects precisely: he thanked God, and took courage. He had already come through Puteoli: “Where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome” (Acts 28:14). The duty is a commandment: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Hebrews 10:25).

webster_full: TAVERN, n. A house licensed to sell liquors in small quantities, to be drank on the spot.

corruption_summary: The gathered church is treated as optional for the mature believer, when the strongest man in the New Testament took courage from the sight of brethren on a road.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word, though the modern sense of tavern misleads careless readers into imagining a scene the text does not describe. The principle to recover is in Luke's two verbs: Paul saw the brethren, and he thanked God, and took courage.

The modern assumption is that the fellowship of the church is a support for weaker Christians and dispensable for the strong. Acts 28:15 is the refutation. The apostle who wrote Romans needed the company of ordinary believers, and God supplied it through men who walked thirty miles of the Appian Way to meet a prisoner. Hebrews makes the gathering a commandment, and notes that some had already made a manner of neglecting it. Those who need it least, if any such exist, are precisely the ones Scripture shows receiving most from it.

etymology: From Old English deman, to judge, from dom, judgment, the root also behind doom and deemster. The Greek huponoeo means to suspect or surmise, from hupo (under) and noeo (to perceive).
biblical_def: In the fourteenth night of the storm off Malta the sailors form a judgment from the sound of the sea: “But when the fourteenth night was come, as we were driven up and down in Adria, about midnight the shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country” (Acts 27:27). To deem is to judge or surmise; the Greek means to suspect, and what follows is the sounding of the lead, twenty fathoms and then fifteen. This is seamanship of a high order, and Luke records it with a sailor's precision. But the ship's safety had already been settled, and not by soundings: “Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me” (Acts 27:25). Paul had the promise; the shipmen had the lead line; and the outcome vindicated both, for God's word was fulfilled through the ordinary labour of men who worked the ship: “And the rest, some on boards, and some on broken pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land” (Acts 27:44). Divine certainty does not retire human diligence; it employs it.

webster_full: DEEM, v.t. To think; to judge; to be of opinion; to conclude on consideration.

corruption_summary: God's decree is set against human action, so that either the promise is used to excuse negligence or diligence is trusted as though no promise had been given.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 27 is the clearest narrative in Scripture on the relation of decree to means, and it is routinely read as if it taught only one of them. The fatalist reading says Paul had the promise, so the soundings and the boats and the cutting of the anchors were irrelevant theatre. The practical atheist reading says the crew saved the ship, and the promise was a pious frame around good seamanship.

Luke writes both into one chapter deliberately. God had promised that not a life would be lost; and Paul tells the centurion that if the sailors escape in the boat the rest cannot be saved, insists that the men eat, and lets the soldiers cut the ropes. The promise was certain and it was fulfilled through fourteen nights of hard work and a timely deeming of the shipmen. Scripture's doctrine of providence establishes means rather than abolishing them, which is why prayer and labour belong in the same hand.

pos: n. (one who sets forth; in the phrase a setter forth of strange gods, a proclaimer of foreign deities)
etymology: Agent noun from set, Old English settan, to place. The phrase renders Greek katangeleus, a proclaimer or announcer, from katangello, to declare. The Athenian charge echoes the one brought against Socrates.
biblical_def: Paul's preaching in the Athenian market draws a technical accusation: “Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection” (Acts 17:18). A setter forth is a proclaimer, and the charge of introducing foreign deities was the same one on which Athens had condemned Socrates four centuries earlier. Luke tells us exactly what provoked it: Paul preached Jesus and the resurrection, and the hearers took Jesus and Anastasis for a pair of new divinities. Paul's answer on Mars' hill does not retreat but turns their own altar against them: “I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” (Acts 17:23). He is not setting forth a strange god but naming the God they had already confessed they did not know, and he ends where every true proclamation ends: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Acts 17:30).

corruption_summary: Paul's Athenian sermon is held up as a model of finding common ground with every religion, when its argument is that the God they confessed as unknown now commands all men everywhere to repent.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17 is the favourite text of religious pluralism and of a certain apologetic style that treats the sermon as a masterclass in affirming other faiths. On that reading Paul finds the Athenians already worshipping the true God under another name, quotes their poets approvingly, and declines to offend. The dictionary rejects it, because the sermon itself does not do what the reading requires.

Paul does begin from their altar and their poets; he is a missionary, not a boor, and starting where hearers stand is apostolic method. But he says they worship ignorantly, tells them God is not worshipped with men's hands, calls their images a product of ignorance that God had overlooked, commands repentance of all men everywhere, and announces a day of judgment by a Man whom God raised from the dead. Common ground was his starting point and never his conclusion. Some mocked, some delayed, and some believed — which is what preaching does.

pos: v. (past participle; appointed as a deputy, commissioned to act for another)
etymology: From Latin deputare, to cut off, to select, hence to appoint, from de and putare, to prune or reckon. To be deputed is to be appointed to act in another's stead. The Hebrew shama here is the verb to hear, used of hearing a cause.
biblical_def: Absalom's conspiracy begins at the city gate with a grievance carefully administered: “And Absalom said unto him, See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee” (2 Samuel 15:3). To be deputed is to be appointed to act for another, and the charge is that David had failed to appoint judges to hear the people's causes. Absalom does not deny the king's right; he exploits the king's neglect. Then comes the offer of himself: “Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!” (2 Samuel 15:4). And the summary verdict of the Spirit: “And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (2 Samuel 15:6). The word is worth an entry because of what it exposes on both sides. Absalom's flattery was wicked, and his complaint was partly true. Unanswered justice in a realm is a door, and ambition will always find it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEPUTE, to appoint as a substitute or agent to act for another; DEPUTED, appointed to act for another.
webster_full: DEPUTE, v.t. To appoint as a substitute or agent to act for another.
To send with a special commission or authority.
DEPUTED, pp. Appointed as a substitute or agent; empowered to act for another.
From Latin deputare, to select or appoint.
2 Samuel 15:3 says there was no man deputed of the king to hear thee.
scriptures: And Absalom said unto him, See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.
Absalom said moreover, Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!
And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
corruption_summary: Grievance is used as a ladder to office, and the men in authority answer the ambition while leaving the real complaint unaddressed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double lesson of 2 Samuel 15: Absalom's method was wicked, and the gap he exploited was genuine.

The demagogue's art has not changed. He meets the aggrieved at the gate, agrees with them before hearing the other side, promises the justice they have not received, and takes their hearts. Churches and institutions produce Absaloms by leaving causes unheard until a flatterer offers to hear them. The remedy is not vigilance against ambition alone but the appointing of men deputed to hear: Moses was told to set rulers over thousands and hundreds, and the apostles appointed deacons the moment a complaint arose. Justice administered promptly leaves ambition nothing to stand on.
roots_summary: Latin deputare, to appoint; 2 Samuel 15:3 is Absalom's charge that no man was deputed of the king to hear.

2 Samuel 15:3 is the only occurrence of deputed in the Authorized Version.

pos: adv. (archaic; inasmuch as, seeing that, because)
etymology: A compound of for, so and much, on the pattern of forasmuch and insomuch. The Greek is kathoti, according as, inasmuch as, from kata and hoti.
biblical_def: Our Lord's verdict on the house of Zacchaeus turns on a single connective: “And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9). Forsomuch means inasmuch as, seeing that; it gives the ground of the declaration. And the ground named is sonship to Abraham — said of a chief publican whom the murmuring crowd had just written off as a sinner. The point is not ethnic descent, which Zacchaeus shared with every critic in the street, but the faith that makes a true son of Abraham: “Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7). Zacchaeus had believed, and the fruit was immediate restitution, fourfold and beyond the law's demand. Then Christ states the principle of His whole ministry: “For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). The little archaic connective carries the doctrine of justification by faith: salvation came to that house because the man in it was, by faith, Abraham's son.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORASMUCH, in consideration that; seeing that; since; FORSOMUCH, the same in sense.
webster_full: FORASMUCH, conj. In consideration that; seeing that; since; it being so that.
FORSOMUCH, in the same sense: inasmuch as; seeing that.
INSOMUCH, so that; to such a degree.
Greek kathoti, according as, inasmuch as.
Luke 19:9 says, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
scriptures: Luk 19:9
And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
Gal 3:7
Know ye therefore that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham.
corruption_summary: Zacchaeus's restitution is made the cause of his salvation rather than its fruit, turning a story of free grace into a transaction.
corruption_paragraphs: A moralising reading of Luke 19 runs thus: Zacchaeus gave back what he had taken, and therefore salvation came to his house. The order is reversed and the gospel lost. Christ had already called him by name, invited Himself to his house, and been received joyfully; the restitution follows the reception, and Christ's declaration follows both, grounded not in the money but in Abrahamic sonship by faith.

The opposite error ignores the restitution altogether, as though grace left the ledger untouched. It does not. Zacchaeus restores fourfold, exceeding what the law required of a thief, and no one commanded him to. That is sanctification beginning the same hour justification is declared — the fruit of faith, never its price. Keep the order and the account preaches both doctrines at once: the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost, and what He saves He changes.
